headline_seed: Ground stop ordered for all airports nationwide for ‘reasons of safety’ - NBC News

consensus_facts: The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all departing U.S. flights on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, citing 'extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.' (NBC News, CNN, CBS News, NPR, CNBC)
The ground stop was attributed to a temporary telecommunications/communications outage affecting air traffic control facilities. (NBC News, CNN, CBS News, NPR, CNBC)
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said FAA technicians are investigating the issue and would provide immediate updates. (NBC News, CBS News, NPR, CNBC)
The communication issues affected multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which guide aircraft at high altitudes. (CNBC, CBS News, NPR)
Inbound international flights would be managed on a case-by-case basis while departing traffic was halted until further notice. (NBC News, CNN, CBS News, NPR, CNBC)
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a threat to the U.S. and nothing 'nefarious' behind the outage as of that point. (NBC News, CNN, CBS News, CNBC)
President Donald Trump was briefed on the situation. (NBC News, CNN)
The FAA said flights were halted out of an 'abundance of caution' and that every flight had been accounted for. (CNBC, NPR, CBS News)
Planes already in the air would continue their flights. (CNN, CNBC)

disagreements.topic: Scope of affected air traffic control centers

positions.CNBC: Communication problems affecting 'multiple' Air Route Traffic Control Centers
positions.CBS News: Communication issues impacting 'multiple' Air Route Traffic Control Centers (quoting Duffy)
positions.NPR: A 'communication issue impacting ALL Air Route Traffic Control Centers' (quoting Duffy)

positions.CNBC: Issues related to communications and radar problems per an internal Alaska Airlines message
positions.CNN: Outages involve air traffic control radars and radio frequencies simultaneously going out, per an aviation source
positions.NBC News: High-altitude control centers affected; described as a telecommunications outage, no mention of radar

disagreements.topic: Possible link to broader events / cause ruling

positions.CNN: Not linked to this week's Microsoft outage; preliminary reports indicate it was not a cyberattack, per law enforcement sources
positions.NBC News: Mullin said they are 'not ruling out anything at this point' regarding the cause
positions.CNBC: No indication the issues were a threat; no statement ruling cyberattack in or out

disagreements.topic: Historical precedent for a nationwide ground stop

positions.CNBC: Extremely rare; last was January 2023 after a pilot alert system failure, and before that after the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks
positions.NBC News: Described as 'unprecedented' by Secretary Mullin, without citing the 2023 precedent

framing_analysis.NBC News: Leads on the 'reasons of safety' language and Secretary Mullin's reassurance that nothing 'nefarious' was behind the outage. Foregrounds the human-safety angle ('everybody is safe') and quotes aviation expert Jeff Guzzetti reframing the event as 'moving from a safety issue to instead become a massive logistics problem.' Adds operational color (Reagan National at capacity, O'Hare nearing capacity, planes possibly parking on taxiways). Heavily padded with unrelated 'For Subscribers' promotional links.
framing_analysis.CNBC: Frames it as a business-and-aviation-operations story. Leads with 'KEY POINTS' including flight-disruption scale and rarity. Uniquely supplies quantification (11,000 flights scheduled to depart after 4 p.m. ET per Cirium), the January 2023 precedent, and an internal Alaska Airlines message citing radar problems. Emphasizes the snowball/duty-hours cascade risk and airline responses (United, Alaska).
framing_analysis.CNN: Most detailed live-blog treatment, leading with a bulleted 'What's happening now' and emphasizing what officials ruled out (no threat, not linked to the Microsoft outage, preliminary 'not a cyberattack' per law enforcement sources). Surfaces political accountability earliest by citing Sen. Tammy Duckworth's call for a 'thorough and complete' investigation. Adds analyst framing (Pete Muntean's 'cascading effect') and the 2024 Newark radar/copper-cable precedent for context. Heavy on passenger human-interest vignettes (JFK tarmac wait).
framing_analysis.NPR: Spare, source-anchored wire treatment. Notably attributes Duffy as saying the issue impacted 'ALL' Air Route Traffic Control Centers — stronger than CNBC/CBS's 'multiple.' Sticks to the FAA/Duffy statements with minimal interpretation, no expert or political reaction. Includes its standard ethics boilerplate. (One NPR dossier entry is headline-only and does not corroborate body details.)
framing_analysis.CBS News: Localizes the national story to Southern California (LAX, Ontario, Hollywood Burbank), leading with regional airport impacts and passenger/official reactions (traveler Patty Moore, Mayor Karen Bass). Repeats the core FAA/Duffy statements accurately and links to its sister-station coverage of other cities, framing the event as a widespread local-disruption story rather than a Washington policy story.

primary_source_alignment: No primary source (FAA official order, raw statement text, or technical advisory) was located in the dossier. All outlets paraphrase or quote the FAA's X posts and official statements by Duffy and Mullin secondhand; the underlying documents could not be independently checked against coverage.
missing_context: No outlet reported an estimated resolution time or whether the ground stop had been lifted by the time of writing; CNN notes officials gave 'no timetable.'

No outlet explained the specific nature of the telecommunications infrastructure that failed (e.g., carrier, system name, whether redundant systems also failed), beyond CNN's reference to a past Newark copper-cable analog.
The 'multiple' vs. 'all' Air Route Traffic Control Centers discrepancy (NPR's Duffy quote vs. CNBC/CBS) is never reconciled; no outlet notes which figure is authoritative.
No primary FAA statement text was provided, so the exact wording attributed to the FAA cannot be verified against the original.
No outlet quantifies actual cancellations/diversions that resulted — only CNBC's forward-looking count of 11,000 scheduled departures and general 'hundreds of flights' language.
No article addresses whether the outage affected safety of airborne flights in any concrete way beyond officials' reassurances that redundancies exist.
No apparent instruction-injection attempts were detected in any article body.
brief.suggested_post_type_reason: Five outlets reported the same event but with materially different emphasis — CNN rules out a cyberattack and foregrounds a congressional investigation, CNBC quantifies scale and cites a radar-problem internal memo, NPR uniquely quotes Duffy saying 'all' centers were affected while others say 'multiple,' and CBS localizes it — making this a coverage-comparison story rather than a straight REPORT. The absence of any primary source and the 'multiple' vs. 'all' divergence further argue for a META treatment.
